text: This is a farmhouse. It was built in the early seventeen-hundreds, on farmland on the edge of Barcelona.
For more than two centuries, nothing special happened here. Then a football club bought the land around it.
And a few decades later, this old house would become the most famous football school in the world — the place that produced Xavi, Iniesta, Busquets, Messi, and now Lamine Yamal.
This is the full story of La Masia.
How it began, the idea that made it different, the generation that conquered the world — and why, after years of doubts, it's producing stars again.
Part one. A house next to a stadium.
The house's real name was Can Planes. The word masia simply means farmhouse in Catalan.

In the nineteen-fifties, Barça bought the land to build the Camp Nou. The old masia ended up right next to the new stadium, and for years it was used as club offices and a workshop for the architects.

Then, in October nineteen seventy-nine, the club turned it into something new: a residence for young players from outside Barcelona — boys who were good enough to join the academy but lived too far away to travel every day.
The idea came from Ajax in Amsterdam, a club Barça had learned a lot from — not least through a certain Dutchman called Johan Cruyff, who had been playing at the Camp Nou a few years earlier.
Generations of players lived there. Then, in twenty eleven, the academy moved to a modern residence at the club's training ground. But the name La Masia stayed with it.
Think about what that meant for a boy of twelve or thirteen. You left your family, your town, your school. You slept in a dormitory next to one of the biggest stadiums in the world.
And every morning, you could look out of the window and see the place you were dreaming of playing in.
Part two. The idea.
For its first years, La Masia was a good academy, but not a unique one. What changed it was a decision taken in nineteen eighty-eight, when Johan Cruyff returned to Barcelona as coach.
Cruyff insisted that every team in the club — from the smallest children to the first team — should play the same way. The same shape, the same ideas, the same priorities.
It sounds obvious now. At the time, it was radical. It meant that a boy who joined at eight years old would spend ten years learning exactly the football he'd be asked to play at the Camp Nou.
The curriculum had a few simple rules. Technique came first. Small, skilful players were valued — which was unusual at a time when many academies picked the biggest and strongest boys.
Every session included the rondo, the passing game in a circle, where the ball must never be lost.
Players were taught to think about space and position: where to stand, when to move, how to create an extra passing option.
And they had to go to school. The club wanted good people, not just good footballers — partly because most academy players never make it to the first team.
Part three. The first harvest.
The first proof arrived quickly. In nineteen ninety, Cruyff promoted a skinny nineteen-year-old from Santpedor to play in the most important position on the pitch, right in front of the defence.
He had lived in La Masia. His name was Pep Guardiola.
Guardiola became the brain of Cruyff's Dream Team, which won Barça's first European Cup in nineteen ninety-two. A boy from the academy was running the best team in Europe.
Behind him came more. Xavi, from Terrassa, who would be compared to Guardiola from the day he arrived.
Carles Puyol, a farm boy from a small town in the Pyrenees, who started as a winger and became one of the great defenders of his era.
Víctor Valdés, the goalkeeper.

And Andrés Iniesta, who arrived from a tiny village in La Mancha at twelve years old. He later said he cried for days when his parents left him at La Masia. Within a few years, the people around him were saying he'd be the best of them all.
Part four. The napkin.
In the year two thousand, a thirteen-year-old boy from Rosario, in Argentina, came to Barcelona for a trial. He was tiny. He needed expensive growth hormone treatment.
Everyone who watched him play knew he was special. But the club took weeks to commit, and his family was running out of patience.
So, on the fourteenth of December, at a restaurant, Barça's sporting director Carles Rexach wrote an agreement on the only thing he had to hand: a paper napkin.
The boy was Lionel Messi. And that napkin became one of the most famous documents in the history of football.

Messi was at the academy at the same time as Gerard Piqué and Cesc Fàbregas. All three were born in nineteen eighty-seven. They played in the same youth team. People still call it the Baby Dream Team.
Piqué and Fàbregas both left for England as teenagers. Both came back years later, as stars. Messi never left — not until twenty twenty-one.
Part five. The peak.

In two thousand and eight, Guardiola, the academy's first great graduate, became first-team coach. And he did something few coaches of a giant club would dare to do: he trusted the academy completely.
He brought up Sergio Busquets and Pedro from the B team. He built his team around Xavi, Iniesta and Messi. In his first season, Barça won everything.

In twenty ten, the three finalists for the Ballon d'Or were Messi, Iniesta and Xavi. All three had come through La Masia. One academy had produced the three best players in the world in the same year.
That same summer, Spain won the World Cup with a team built around Barça's academy players. Iniesta scored the winner in the final.

And then came a moment that may never be repeated. On the twenty-fifth of November, twenty twelve, away at Levante, Dani Alves was substituted early in the game. His replacement was Martín Montoya, from the academy.
For the rest of that match, all eleven Barcelona players on the pitch were La Masia graduates. At the highest level of football, one club was playing an entire team it had grown itself.
Part six. The drought.
But after that peak, something went wrong. As the great generation got older, the club started spending enormous sums on transfers instead of trusting its youngsters.
Talented academy players found the path to the first team blocked by expensive signings. Many left for other clubs. Some became stars elsewhere.
For several years, people asked whether La Masia's magic was over — whether the world had copied its ideas so well that Barça no longer had an advantage.
Part seven. The return.

The answer came from the worst possible situation. When the money ran out, Barça had no choice but to trust their academy again. Gavi made his debut at seventeen. Alejandro Balde became a starter at left-back.
Fermín López scored in big games. Marc Casadó stepped into the midfield.
Pau Cubarsí became a first-team centre-back at seventeen, playing with a calmness that reminded people of Piqué and Puyol.

And then there was Lamine Yamal — a European champion at sixteen, runner-up for the Ballon d'Or at eighteen. A boy who, as a baby, had been photographed with Messi for a charity calendar. The circle had closed.
Today, the original farmhouse is no longer where the young players sleep. The academy has modern buildings, gyms, video rooms and classrooms.
But La Masia was never really about a building. It was about an idea: that a club could grow its own players, teach them one way of playing from the age of eight, and trust them on the biggest stage.
It's an idea that came from Amsterdam, was perfected in Barcelona, and changed how the whole world thinks about youth football. And after a long pause, it's working again.
So who is the greatest La Masia graduate of all time? Messi, Iniesta, Xavi — or someone else? Tell me in the comments.
And for the man whose idea made all of this possible, watch The Full Story of Johan Cruyff.
